item.title: HomeView and new Apple TV 4K launch today
item.description:
Apple's two big home products are officially out today: the all-new HomeView smart display ($299) and the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K, both announced October 13 and now shipping to pre-order customers and on sale in Apple Stores. HomeView is Apple's first smart home display, powered by Siri AI, with a 7-inch screen that recognizes up to six users by face and gives each a personalized home screen. Apple also published support guides and release notes for HomeView software 27.2, covering facial recognition, multiuser profiles, and repairs — plus the caveat that it may not recognize you in sunglasses.

Early impressions are mixed but enthusiastic: reviewers praise the build quality, sound, and a record-low 0.3-nit minimum brightness that suits a bedside table, while questioning how much it adds to a home already full of Apple devices. Apple executives told TechRadar the design was a "hard fought, fun journey" balancing audio, privacy, and Siri AI. The new Apple TV 4K brings the A19 chip, Siri AI, an updated Siri Remote with Find My, and four-speaker surround support.

item.title: Siri AI reaches older Apple TV 4K models — but not HomePod mini 2
item.description:
Apple released tvOS 27.2.1 today, bringing Siri AI to the second- and third-generation Apple TV 4K models from 2021 and 2022. A paired Siri AI-enabled device nearby is required, since the older boxes can't run it on their own. The update had been conspicuously absent when Apple shipped its other 27.2.1 updates earlier in the week — apparently held back to coincide with the new Apple TV 4K launch.

Meanwhile, the HomePod mini 2 is still waiting: today's HomePod software 27.2.1 does not enable Siri AI on the new speaker, and Apple's site still says only "coming in a future software update" with no timeframe. The mini 2 has just 2GB of RAM, well below the 8GB minimum for on-device Siri AI, so personal-context requests will need a paired Apple Intelligence iPhone or iPad. Some new Apple TV 4K owners hit a YouTube app error; the fix is to install tvOS 27.2, restart, or reinstall the app.

item.title: Epic asks Supreme Court to uphold contempt ruling against Apple
item.description:
Epic Games has filed its formal response to Apple's Supreme Court appeal, urging the justices to uphold the contempt ruling over App Store payment restrictions. Epic argues Apple complied with the letter of the judge's steering order — allowing developers to link out to alternative payment options — while undermining its spirit with fees and friction that kept the old system effectively intact.

The filing sets up the next chapter of the long-running saga: oral arguments are scheduled for January 11, 2027. The stakes are the App Store's payment rules and the tens of billions in commissions they generate, so the Court's decision could reshape how iOS apps take payments in the US for years to come.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: Epic formally asks SCOTUS to uphold contempt ruling against Apple
  • AppleInsider: Epic wants Apple punished for following letter but not spirit of the ruling

item.title: Microsoft 365 outage nears 24 hours, now resolving
item.description:
A global Microsoft 365 outage that began around 1 p.m. Eastern on Thursday knocked out Outlook email and disrupted Teams, Copilot, and other services for nearly a full day, with almost 130,000 Outlook reports logged on Downdetector shortly after it started. Exchange Online was at the center of it, and Exchange accounts in Apple Mail were affected too.

By Friday evening Microsoft said the underlying issue was fixed and it was seeing "broad recovery and stability" as it restored access. Microsoft blamed failed server health checks, not hackers, and extended email timeouts to 48 hours to preserve delayed mail during the disruption. It hit businesses and government operations, with Japan confirming a significant impact on its government IT systems.

item.title: iPhone Duo survives 450,000 folds — and tops 100,000 apps
item.description:
CNET's three-week hinge stress test of the iPhone Duo has passed 451,000 folds, and the phone still works — though the hinge is showing wear. It started feeling looser around 390,000 folds, and by 440,300 the mechanism had shifted enough that the screen stopped 5 to 10 degrees short of fully open, with the distinctive snap gone. It can still be opened fully by hand.

Apple also says more than 100,000 apps have now been built for the Duo — though many are simple refactors rather than apps fully redesigned for the big foldable display, and developers warn it will take time before favorite apps really take advantage of it.

item.title: iPhone 18 and 18e coming spring 2027 with A20 chip
item.description:
Apple's iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e will launch in spring 2027 with the new A20 chip, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reiterated on the latest episode of his "Power On" podcast, in line with his earlier reporting. The iPhone Air 2 is expected at the same time.

The timing confirms Apple's split launch cadence: the Pro models arrive in the fall, while the standard iPhone 18, the budget 18e, and the Air 2 follow the next spring. That puts the base iPhone 18 roughly six months behind the iPhone 18 Pro, a staggered schedule that would have been unthinkable a few years ago but now looks like Apple's settled rhythm.

item.title: First Apple Home Collection accessories now available to order
item.description:
Alongside HomeView itself, the first three accessories in the Apple Home Collection are now available to order: LG's Indoor Cam ($199.95), Outdoor Cam ($299.95), and Video Doorbell ($249.95), all designed to work natively with Apple's home platform and due to ship in December. Apple is listing nine smart home devices plus accessories such as adapters in total, but only these three are orderable so far.

The rest of the lineup, from LG and Schneider Home, is expected to launch by early 2027. The cameras and doorbell are positioned as a more private, HomeKit-native alternative to the likes of Ring — a pitch likely to appeal to Apple users already deep in the ecosystem.

item.title: Apple meets Thai officials over spyware warnings
item.description:
Apple met with Thai officials earlier this week to discuss spyware warnings sent to politicians and other users in the country, Bloomberg reports. The talks followed Apple's October 29 threat notifications, which reached users in 99 countries after Apple identified activity consistent with mercenary spyware attacks, raising concerns about surveillance of Thai political figures.

Thailand's Digital Economy and Society Minister Chaichanok Chidchob said after the meeting that the alerts alone do not establish that attackers actually succeeded in compromising devices. The episode is a reminder that Apple's threat notifications — now sent to users in nearly a hundred countries — are a warning of targeted attack activity, not confirmation of a successful hack.

Sources

item.title: HomeView launches tomorrow as reviews land: charming but unfinished
item.description:
Apple's first smart home display, the HomeView, arrives Friday, November 13, with the first pre-orders already reaching customers in Australia and New Zealand. Reviews are warm but measured: The Verge calls it powerful enough to run a smart home, MacStories rounds up praise for a simple, charming device built for Apple users, and 9to5Mac says it earns its place — while AppleInsider sees a shallow launch with incredible potential and Six Colors a late arrival still showing seams.

The launch is already a bit messy. Apple has pushed out a day-zero software update fixing nine security vulnerabilities, and a December update is promised to fix Siri glitches — including Siri once claiming the device has no camera, and refusing to open a garage door or unlock a front door it recognized the owner for. The first Apple Home Collection accessories — LG indoor and outdoor cameras and a video doorbell — go on sale Friday for December delivery. Apple also detailed how Secure Exclaves isolate the HomeView's camera and microphone data from the rest of the system.

item.title: New Apple TV 4K arrives Friday with Siri AI — and older models get it too
item.description:
The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K launches Friday, four years after its predecessor, and reviewers agree on the verdict: it's the best streamer you can buy, at a price that's hard to justify. The new box starts at $299 and pairs an A19 chip with Siri AI, a faster experience, and an improved remote.

MacRumors' hands-on found Siri AI noticeably better than the old Siri at pulling up recommendations and answering questions about content, though it's still in beta and struggles with follow-up questions. AppleInsider calls the price tag eye-watering. Good news for existing owners: an upcoming tvOS 27.2.1 update will bring Siri AI to the second- and third-generation Apple TV 4K models as well, so the headline feature isn't exclusive to the new hardware.

item.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns in disgrace; Trump taps Tim Cook, Srouji eyed as successor
item.description:
Nvidia announced that co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang has resigned effective immediately, after reports of multiple extramarital affairs — including one with a woman U.S. intelligence suspects of spying for China. The board had initially backed him, but moved after a second affair surfaced and the company's market value fell by more than $800 billion. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement, and Huang has agreed to testify before Congress behind closed doors by Thanksgiving.

The story keeps looping back to Apple. President Trump posted that Tim Cook should be Nvidia's next CEO, calling him the only man for the job. Separately, Semafor reports that Apple's chief hardware officer Johny Srouji — the architect of the move from Intel to Apple silicon — is among the candidates under consideration, though it's unclear whether he has been approached or would be interested.

item.title: Apple TV debuts three new originals and lines up a Brad Pitt film
item.description:
Apple TV subscribers can now watch three new originals: a heist thriller series, a film based on true events, and the first of two holiday specials arriving this season. Apple also announced two more projects in the pipeline.

The bigger news is a reunion with Brad Pitt, the star of Apple's most successful film to date. Pitt will star in "Connector," a film about a legendary ironworker in 1970s New York who takes on forces greater than himself, written by Darius Marder and Nina Marder, with Pitt executive producing through Plan B. It's still in development with no release date. And the comedy "She's Fine," starring Elizabeth Banks as a recent divorcee starting over — alongside Ted Danson, Rob Delaney, and Katey Sagal — premieres January 27.

item.title: iPhone Duo delivery dates are moving up — but a reader poll says 30% returned it
item.description:
Some iPhone Duo buyers who were facing a January 25 delivery date are now seeing their orders arrive December 14–21, with a few moved up as far as December 12–14 — though Apple's store still quotes January 25 for new orders. Meanwhile, a 9to5Mac reader poll of early buyers found about 30% have returned the device, a figure the site's author argues isn't surprising or worrying for a first-generation foldable.

The broader picture stays bullish: Foxconn's revenue climbed 46% year over year on consumer electronics and server demand, Bloomberg Intelligence forecasts 16 million iPhone Duo sales in the first 12 months, and China Renaissance raised its Apple price target to $425 — up more than 50% — betting the foldable sparks a major upgrade cycle, despite limited evidence that early demand will hold.

item.title: Nvidia board reportedly preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang
item.description:
Nvidia's board is reportedly preparing to oust CEO and founder Jensen Huang as soon as Wednesday, after a second extramarital affair came to light. The New York Times reported that Huang also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports to him — a potential violation of the company's code of conduct. That followed an earlier report that Huang had an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence determined is a suspected Chinese spy.

The board has been working with an outside firm to identify CEO candidates and is weighing naming an interim chief while it searches for a permanent replacement, with CFO Colette Kress reportedly favored by some directors for the interim role. Directors were set to meet Wednesday to decide Huang's future, and the board has briefed the White House on its planned meeting. Huang's departure would end the era in which he drove the global AI boom and made Nvidia the world's most valuable company.

item.title: Apple abruptly shutters its Support Community forums
item.description:
Apple abruptly placed the Apple Support Community into a read-only state on Tuesday and announced the forums will permanently close on Friday, November 20. Contributors — some of whom volunteered on the site for more than two decades — were blindsided, with no chance to post farewell messages.

Reactions were mixed. Jason Snell called the boards an embarrassment for Apple, outdated and misleadingly official-looking under an apple.com domain, and said good riddance. Others noted the forums, for all their generic point-chasing answers, were sometimes genuinely useful, and that the volunteers deserved a proper goodbye. The forums will remain online as a searchable archive of answers, but no new questions or discussions will be possible.

item.title: Apple employee charged after fatal crash near Apple Park kills toddler
item.description:
Apple employee Eric Chen Su was arrested and charged with suspicion of gross vehicular manslaughter following a fatal collision near the Apple Park Visitor Center on Friday. Shortly after noon, Su was reportedly traveling between 90 and 100 miles per hour when he struck the back of a stopped vehicle occupied by a two-year-old girl and her babysitter. Both were seriously injured and taken to a hospital; the child, Riley Howard, died, while the babysitter survived. Su sustained light injuries.

Apple said in a statement that its hearts are broken, and the incident has shaken the community around its Cupertino campus. The crash occurred at the intersection of North Tantau Avenue and Pruneridge Avenue, right next to the Visitor Center.

item.title: iPhone Duo, one week in: impressive, but not for everyone
item.description:
A week after launch, the first long-term verdicts on Apple's folding iPhone Duo are landing — and they're mixed. Photographer Austin Mann found it genuinely special, saying it shines in everything around the photograph: planning, editing, and sharing. Quinn Nelson's review, meanwhile, argues the Duo "doesn't feel like an iPhone." Camera testing found a capable system that lags the Pro iPhones in extreme low light and misses some pro features.

The question many reviewers keep circling is whether the Duo is the iPhone's future or simply not for everyone. Some early buyers have reportedly returned their devices after the novelty wore off, and 9to5Mac is polling readers on whether they kept or returned theirs. For most people, the regular iPhones remain the safer pick.

item.title: Binance warns iPhone users of unpatched iOS exploit that can steal data from other apps
item.description:
Crypto exchange Binance is warning iPhone users about an iOS vulnerability that researchers say remains unpatched and could allow a malicious app to access sensitive data stored by other apps on the device. In a post on X on November 10, Binance flagged the flaw as affecting multiple iOS versions, including iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2.

The warning matters most to crypto holders, since finance apps are prime targets for data theft, but the underlying issue is broader: a malicious app could potentially reach data used by other apps. Details of the exploit itself remain sparse in the reports. Until Apple ships a fix, the practical advice is the usual — only install apps from trusted developers and keep iOS updated when patches arrive.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: Binance warns iPhone crypto holders of security flaw researchers say remains unpatched

item.title: Google Gemini arrives on Apple CarPlay
item.description:
Google announced Wednesday that a dedicated Gemini app is rolling out on Apple CarPlay worldwide in several languages, starting today. Drivers can tap the Gemini icon on the CarPlay display or side rail to start or resume a conversation, with Gemini Live supporting back-and-forth voice chats — including interrupting, changing the subject, or pausing mid-conversation.

Conversations on the iPhone sync to CarPlay, so a chat started at home can continue on the road. Gemini can pull from your Google apps to give a personalized daily brief, catch you up on unread emails, or tell you when your next appointment starts — and help find a restaurant while driving. It's a notable moment: Google's AI assistant now has a first-class seat on Apple's in-car platform.

item.title: Supplier earnings briefing points to Apple AI glasses and camera AirPods
item.description:
Apple's long-rumored smart glasses and AirPods with cameras got fresh corroboration from an unexpected source: a Chinese supplier's quarterly earnings briefing. Quick Intelligent Equipment, a manufacturing equipment supplier, said it has been involved in "Apple's AI glasses and new smart earphones projects," which it expects to boost demand for its machine-vision inspection equipment.

Apple is reportedly targeting a late 2027 launch for its first smart glasses, expected to answer questions about the wearer's surroundings and translate languages. The supplier's candor is unusual — most firms avoid spoiling Apple's future product plans in earnings calls — and it adds weight to the idea that both wearables are actively in development rather than distant concepts.

item.title: iPhone 18 Pro Max tops CNET battery test of 32 smartphones
item.description:
Apple's iPhone 18 Pro Max placed first overall in CNET's battery comparison of 32 smartphones, with other iPhone models also leading individual tests and matching significantly more expensive devices. CNET ran two tests totaling three hours and 45 minutes: three hours of video streaming over Wi-Fi at maximum brightness, plus 45 minutes mixing video playback, video calls, gaming, and social media. Each phone started at 100 percent charge, and the publication averaged the remaining percentages for its overall rankings.

The result is a strong showing for Apple's battery life across the iPhone 18 lineup — not just the flagship — and a useful data point for anyone weighing an upgrade this holiday season.

item.title: Apple Support Community forums to close permanently on November 20
item.description:
Apple announced that its long-running Apple Support Community discussion forums will permanently close on Friday, November 20. The forums went read-only immediately, with new posts no longer accepted; the final post appears to have been submitted Tuesday afternoon Pacific time.

Apple gave no reason for the closure. The likely explanation is that users have migrated to communities like Reddit and Discord, and to AI-assisted support, while Apple itself increasingly uses AI to parse support queries. The forums were a decades-old trove of peer troubleshooting for Mac, iPhone, and other Apple products, so their disappearance removes a major public archive of fixes — though the site remains readable until the shutdown date.

item.title: Some PROLED MacBook Pro owners report eye strain and headaches
item.description:
Some buyers of the new touchscreen PROLED MacBook Pro report eye strain, headaches, and dizziness, and the culprit appears to be pulse width modulation — the technique the display uses to control brightness by rapidly strobing the backlight. At certain brightness levels the combination of flicker frequency and amplitude is enough to bother sensitive users, even though the strobing is far too fast to see consciously.

Not everyone is affected, and susceptibility varies widely, but for those who are, the usual mitigations apply: raising brightness, which typically reduces the modulation depth, or using the machine with an external display. It is an early blemish on an otherwise well-received redesign, and one worth knowing about before buying.

Sources

  • AppleInsider News: If you're getting dizzy using PROLED MacBook Pro, you are not alone

item.title: iFixit teardown reveals how the glowing Apple logo works
item.description:
iFixit tore down the new touchscreen PROLED MacBook Pro and showed how Apple brought back the glowing logo on the lid. With no display backlight to borrow, Apple uses four LEDs, a reflective layer, and a diffuser to produce an even glow, while a two-way mirror coating gives the logo a shiny finish when the light is off.

The teardown also found the machine more repairable overall, but the logo itself is not a friendly repair: it sits behind the display, so a broken logo effectively means removing the screen. It is a nostalgic callback with a thoroughly modern, and somewhat impractical, implementation.

item.title: Apple's Claris is testing Harbor, an app to run local AI across Macs
item.description:
Apple's Claris subsidiary is testing an app called Harbor that turns Apple silicon Macs into a private AI server, letting users browse for, download, and load open-weight models with no manual configuration. A single Mac works, but Harbor can also link several Macs over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory for larger models — something macOS Tahoe 26.2 enables with RDMA over Thunderbolt 5.

The appeal is privacy and simplicity: models run locally, so data never leaves your machines, and the setup that normally requires command-line tooling becomes a consumer app. No release date has been announced, but it signals Apple taking local, on-device AI seriously.

item.title: Swift Student Challenge 2027 opens to apps on any Apple platform
item.description:
Apple announced the Swift Student Challenge for 2027, with submissions open from February 8 to February 28. The big change this year: students can submit an app for any Apple platform, not just iOS and iPadOS as in prior years — so Mac, Apple Watch, Apple TV, and Vision Pro entries are all fair game.

As before, students build an app in Xcode or Swift Playgrounds that can be experienced within three minutes, and winners are celebrated in the run-up to WWDC. Apple is also offering preparatory resources ahead of the contest. The expansion reflects how Swift development now spans the whole ecosystem, and it gives students far more room to show off what they can build.

item.title: Apple TV adds sign language interpretation starting Friday
item.description:
Apple announced a new accessibility feature for the Apple TV app: sign language interpretation for supported movies and shows, launching Friday, November 13, with the new film Being Heumann. An interpreter appears in the bottom-right corner, with the experience designed and tested by Deaf and native signers.

American Sign Language and British Sign Language will be available at launch, with more titles to follow. The feature requires iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS 27.2, tvOS 27.2, or visionOS 27.2 or later, and supported titles will show a Sign Language icon. Unlike rivals that ship separate signed versions of films, Apple bakes interpretation into the regular playback experience — a meaningful step for Deaf viewers.

item.title: OLED iPad Air still expected in early 2027, in both sizes
item.description:
A new DigiTimes supply-chain report backs an OLED iPad Air launching in the first half of 2027, with OLED panels in both the 11-inch and 13-inch sizes. Samsung Display is expected to supply most panels, with BOE seeking orders for one of the two sizes. The OLED upgrade has been rumored for over a year, and Bloomberg's Mark Gurman narrowed the window to the first half of 2027 earlier this month.

The next iPad Air is also expected to borrow from last month's iPad mini refresh: an M5 chip, thinner bezels, and possibly a nano-texture display option. The display would likely stay at 60Hz, keeping ProMotion exclusive to the iPad Pro. For buyers weighing an iPad Air now, the message is consistent: a substantially better screen is coming, but not until next year.

item.title: Three workers die at Tata iPhone parts plant in India
item.description:
Three contract workers died Monday at a Tata Electronics facility in Hosur, Tamil Nadu, that makes components for the iPhone. The workers were performing maintenance at a wastewater treatment plant when they inhaled gas while inspecting a nano-filtration tank. The plant was operated by Nalco Water, and the workers were employed by a subcontractor.

Apple said it is sending a team to assist in the investigation, alongside Tata Electronics and state officials. The incident did not affect production. The facility has previously faced scrutiny over environmental concerns, and the deaths put fresh focus on safety oversight in Apple's India supply chain as manufacturing there continues to expand.

Sources

item.title: Apple ships iOS 27.2.1 and macOS 27.2.1 with fixes for iMessage snooping and rogue Bluetooth pairing
item.description:
Apple released a round of point updates across nearly every platform — iOS 27.2.1, iPadOS 27.2.1, macOS Golden Gate 27.2.1, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1 — and the fixes are genuinely worth installing promptly. Several iMessage flaws could have let a remote attacker join a group chat to read its messages, or let users see messages sent before they joined. Most of the remaining bugs involved AirPlay and Bluetooth, including one that allowed a malicious Bluetooth device to pair without user interaction and another that let a nearby attacker corrupt process memory.

The macOS update also closes a gap around compromised eMudhra certificates: Apple had blocked them in Safari, Mail, and other apps in October, but command-line tools like curl and git still accepted them until now. Apple also pushed security-only updates for older systems — iOS 26.7.3, macOS Tahoe 26.7.3, and macOS Sequoia 15.8.3.

item.title: Apple starts charging for heavy AI use with $50 'intelligence usage packs'
item.description:
Apple has taken its first real step toward charging for Apple Intelligence. Users of Apple Creator Studio who hit the monthly usage limits on AI features in apps like Logic Pro can now buy $50 'intelligence usage packs' for extra capacity. It follows months of Apple quietly noting in press releases that server-side Private Cloud Compute features have daily limits, with expanded access 'available for a fee in the future.'

For now the paid packs are limited to Creator Studio users, and Apple has said expanded access will eventually be bundled with select iCloud+ plans rather than sold standalone. But the direction of travel is clear: the free tier of Apple's AI is capped, and heavy users will pay. No pricing or timing has been announced for the broader rollout.

item.title: Canadian court certifies class action against Apple over its Google search deal
item.description:
A British Columbia Supreme Court judge has certified a class action against Apple alleging that its search agreement with Google stifled competition and inflated advertising prices. The suit claims a deal struck between Apple and Google in 2005 locked rival search engines out of the market — a familiar regulatory target, but framed here as a conspiracy claim that even sympathetic coverage describes as a peculiar angle.

Certification doesn't mean the plaintiffs have won; it just means the case can proceed as a class action toward trial. Still, it adds to the pile of legal pressure on the Apple-Google arrangement, which has already drawn scrutiny from regulators on both sides of the border.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: Canadian court certifies class action against Apple over Google search deal
  • AppleInsider: Conspiratorial Canadian search engine class action lawsuit against Apple going forward

item.title: Apple Intelligence clears regulatory registration for iPad and Mac in China
item.description:
Apple has completed an important regulatory step ahead of Apple Intelligence's expected launch in China this December. According to China's cyberspace regulator, Apple has now registered Apple Intelligence for use on tablets and notebooks — meaning iPads and Macs, not just iPhones. The iOS 27.3 developer beta brought Apple Intelligence to China on iPhone after a two-year wait behind the rest of the world, and the new registration suggests the broader rollout is close behind.

China is one of Apple's largest markets and one of the most tightly regulated for AI, so clearing this hurdle matters commercially as well as symbolically. The December launch will be the first time Chinese users get the full Apple Intelligence experience across their devices.

item.title: Apple announces major Türkiye investment: five Developer Academies and its first manufacturing academy outside the US
item.description:
Apple announced a long-term investment in Türkiye as Tim Cook toured the country, meeting retail employees, app developers, content creators, and an athlete. The plan includes seven new facilities: five Apple Developer Academies, a Developer Center in Istanbul, and an Advanced Manufacturing Center in Ankara — the first manufacturing academy Apple has opened outside the US. The academies will roll out over the next three years, with the first opening in Istanbul in 2027, offering free coding courses and advanced manufacturing training.

The move is part of Apple's broader push to grow its developer ecosystem and manufacturing footprint beyond its traditional hubs. Türkiye has a large, young developer community, and the investment signals Apple sees it as a meaningful market for both app development and manufacturing talent.

item.title: Report: Apple saved over $5 billion in taxes through Singapore and Ireland in 2026
item.description:
A Financial Times report digging into Apple's annual report found the company saved more than $5 billion in taxes in fiscal 2026 by routing profits through Singapore and Ireland. Apple paid $4.96 billion in cash income taxes in Ireland and $3.25 billion in Singapore. Against the 21% US federal corporate tax rate, Singapore alone lowered Apple's tax expense by $2.67 billion — about $100 million more than Ireland did.

The numbers also show the limits of the strategy: Singapore's lower rate and incentives would have saved Apple $5.49 billion before other taxes and adjustments, but a $2.51 billion top-up tax erased nearly half of that saving. Singapore introduced the top-up tax to bring multinationals' effective rates closer to the global minimum, and the figures suggest it's starting to bite.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: Report: Apple saved over $5 billion in taxes through Singapore and Ireland in 2026

item.title: Apple Stores ordered to stop signing up customers to services without consent
item.description:
Apple has reportedly directed all of its retail stores to stop signing up customers to services such as Apple TV without their knowledge, after the practice was exposed by repair technician and consumer rights advocate Louis Rossmann. Store staff reported being pressured into enrolling customers in subscriptions, and Apple has taken two steps indicating it takes the accusations seriously — though the company has not publicly commented on the allegations.

The story is awkward for Apple, which has previously cracked down on other companies pushing subscriptions on unwitting users. Whether Apple expressly sanctioned the practice or simply created sales pressure that led employees to cut corners, the episode shows the same dark patterns Apple criticizes in others can emerge from aggressive services targets. No specific stores have been identified.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: Apple staff accused of signing up customers to subscriptions without consent; company responds

item.title: Some HomePod mini 2 buyers are returning units over broken Mac speaker feature
item.description:
One of the headline features of Apple's new HomePod mini 2 — using it as your Mac's default speaker — isn't working reliably for a number of buyers, and some are already returning their units, according to MacRumors forum reports. A single HomePod mini 2 can be used alone, or a pair can be twinned for stereo sound, on any Mac with Wi-Fi 6E or later.

The same feature never worked reliably on the first-generation HomePod mini either, which makes the repeat disappointing for a product whose main selling point over its predecessor is exactly this capability. It's early days and the reports are anecdotal, so it's unclear how widespread the problem is — but anyone who bought the mini 2 specifically to replace their Mac speakers should test the feature inside the return window.

Sources

  • MacRumors: Some HomePod Mini 2 Buyers Returning Units Over Mac Speaker Issues

item.title: Apple Store employees accused of signing customers up for subscriptions without consent
item.description:
Consumer rights advocate Louis Rossmann has accused some Apple Store employees of enrolling customers in auto-renewing subscription trials — including Apple One — without their informed consent, in a series of YouTube videos posted over the past two weeks. The alleged pattern starts with an employee offering to scan a QR code for a personalized shopping experience called "Connect and Personalize." That flow, Rossmann claims, can end with customers unknowingly signed up for paid trials.

The accusations land at a sensitive moment for Apple, which leans heavily on services revenue and markets itself on user trust. Apple has not yet publicly responded in the coverage. If the claims hold up, expect scrutiny of the in-store signup flow and whether the company tightens how employees present trials — or faces regulatory attention over consent practices at retail.

Sources

  • MacRumors: Apple Store Subscription Sign-Up Controversy Exposed

item.title: Nvidia opens investigation into CEO Jensen Huang after relationship with alleged Chinese spy
item.description:
Nvidia announced Sunday that it is investigating its chief executive and co-founder, Jensen Huang, after he acknowledged to the board that he had been intimate with a business executive whom U.S. intelligence determined to be a Chinese spy. The woman, named Alice Huang, was under surveillance that reportedly showed her feeding information directly to Beijing.

The fallout goes beyond a personal scandal: Huang is one of the most powerful figures in the global chip industry, and Nvidia's chips sit at the center of U.S.-China technology tensions. Nvidia says it does not share classified information with customers and denies Huang pressed the government to change chip export policy. The investigation is now underway, and the episode is likely to draw further attention to how U.S. intelligence views the company's China relationships.

Sources

  • Daring Fireball: Jensen Huang Betrayed Nvidia, Not Just His Family
  • Daring Fireball: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Was Banging a Chinese Spy, Who Was Feeding Information Back to Beijing

item.title: Siri could become "more like an agent" as early as next year
item.description:
Apple's long-awaited personalized Siri finally shipped with iOS 27, but it still doesn't proactively take actions for users the way rival agents do. That may change soon: Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports Apple could make Siri function "more like an agent" as early as next year, able to keep track of goals, figure out what needs to happen next, and keep pursuing objectives without being prompted step by step.

The timeline is still gradual. Siri AI in the iOS 27.3 developer beta can already handle more tasks in first-party apps, but deeper control of Apple apps — and any expansion to third-party apps — isn't expected until spring 2027. The direction is clear, though: Apple is moving Siri from a command-response assistant toward a proactive agent, even if it's arriving later than competitors.

item.title: New CEO John Ternus is pushing to speed up Apple's software — and the Siri chief may leave
item.description:
New Apple CEO John Ternus is reportedly pressing software chief Craig Federighi to accelerate Apple's software roadmap, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman — the latest sign that the company's pace in AI has become a top-level concern. The pressure comes as Apple faces persistent criticism that it is moving too slowly to keep up with rivals.

At the same time, Mike Rockwell — who led the Vision Pro and then took over Siri AI for its 2026 revamp — is reportedly considering stepping down from the Siri role during 2027, or leaving Apple altogether. Gurman also notes differing views among leadership about AI strategy. Taken together, the reports suggest Apple's AI leadership is in flux at the very moment the new CEO is demanding faster results.

item.title: Apple is changing how it builds iOS 28 and macOS 28 to give engineers more room to create
item.description:
Apple has reworked its development schedule for iOS 28, macOS 28, and the rest of next year's operating systems. The company typically splits each year's OS development into three stages of four weeks of coding followed by four weeks of "convergence," where features get integrated. For the 28 generation, the first stage stretched to six weeks of coding, giving engineers more creative time before the convergence crunch.

The tweak may sound bureaucratic, but the way work is scheduled shapes what gets built — more uninterrupted coding time early on could mean more ambitious features, or at least fewer half-finished ones. It's also a practical response to the same pressure behind the Ternus push: Apple wants its software teams moving faster without sacrificing quality.

Sources

  • MacRumors: Apple Taking New Approach to Developing iOS 28 and macOS 28
  • AppleInsider: Apple's iOS 28 schedule shift helps engineers get more creative

item.title: Apple saved $2.7B in taxes this year by routing finances through Singapore
item.description:
Apple saved $2.7 billion in taxes in 2026 by funneling its finances through Singapore, according to a Financial Times report based on an annual Apple disclosure filed under U.S. reporting rules. Ireland has long been Apple's best-known tax-efficient hub, but Singapore's incentives delivered an even better result this year.

For a company of Apple's scale, tax strategy is as much a part of the financial story as product sales — and the Singapore route shows how multinationals keep shifting structures as rules and incentives change. Expect the disclosure to draw the usual questions from regulators and tax watchdogs, even though the arrangement is legal under current rules.

Sources

  • AppleInsider: Apple saves $2.7B in taxes by funnelling finances through Singapore

item.title: macOS 27.3 may rein in AI agents asking for Full Disk Access
item.description:
Apple announced last month it would tighten privacy controls in a future macOS update after AI agents began requesting Full Disk Access and then using users' data in ways they hadn't fully understood. Now there's a first look at how the changes might work in macOS 27.3, with a more explicit, granular permission flow for agents requesting broad access to your files.

The move matters because AI agents are increasingly asking for the keys to the kingdom — full disk access — to do their jobs, and the old one-tap grant didn't make the stakes clear. A stricter, clearer flow should keep users from accidentally handing an agent access to everything on their Mac, while still letting power users who know what they're doing opt in.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: macOS 27.3 could change how you grant AI agents Full Disk Access, here’s how

item.title: Apple launched five products this week, with two more on the way
item.description:
Apple is having a very busy November. Five new products launched on Friday, November 6, following pre-orders that opened the week before, and two more products are still on tap for next week. On the software side, Apple released the first betas of iOS 27.3 and related updates, bringing a number of tweaks and new features.

The pace is notable even by Apple's standards — a week into November and the company is still rolling out hardware. Looking further ahead, the pipeline for the first half of 2027 is already taking shape, with more product launches expected in the coming months. For anyone holding off on a purchase, the flood of new hardware also means the previous generation is about to get cheaper, which ties into the early Black Friday deals already surfacing.

item.title: iPhone Air 2 arrives next spring with a second camera — and more to prove
item.description:
Apple will unveil the second-generation iPhone Air next spring, after taking extra time to rework the design and add a second camera. But the phone's position in the lineup has changed since the first Air launched: the iPhone Duo foldable is now the flashy, attention-grabbing device, and the Air can no longer coast on being the cool one.

That means the Air 2 has to appeal to a much wider audience than just enthusiasts drawn to its thinness. The added camera addresses one of the original's most obvious compromises, but the real question is whether Apple can give the Air a clear reason to exist alongside the Duo and the standard iPhone. Spring is still months away, so expect more details to leak before the announcement.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: iPhone Air 2 is coming next year, here’s why it has more to prove than ever

item.title: Chromagraph Camera brings a film look to iPhone photos
item.description:
Movie director Rian Johnson surprised everyone last week by launching Chromagraph Camera, a new iPhone camera app that reimagines what a smartphone photo should look like. The pitch is simple: iPhone photos tend to look overprocessed, and while the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo's new film texture option helps, it goes a bit too far in the other direction.

Chromagraph lands in the sweet spot, according to early hands-on impressions — a film-like look that feels natural rather than exaggerated. For anyone who has been frustrated by the computational, over-sharpened feel of default iPhone photos, this is the most promising third-party camera app to arrive in a while, and it comes from a filmmaker who clearly cares about the image.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: Chromagraph Camera is exactly the camera app I’ve been looking for on iPhone

item.title: New MacBook Pros get a glowing logo — and a free app to control it
item.description:
The new MacBook Pros brought back the glowing Apple logo on the lid, and designer Juan Buis has already shipped an app to control it. Backglow lets you adjust the logo's brightness independently of the display, turn it off entirely with one click instead of resorting to Terminal, or enable a "Breathe" mode that gently pulses the light like the sleep indicator on older MacBooks. The free version covers all of that; a one-time $9 payment unlocks the Pro features.

Meanwhile, the new machines themselves continue to draw attention — John Gruber joined Tyler Stalman and David Altizer's Full Stack Creator show this week to talk about the new MacBook Pros and their PROLED XDR displays, which he covered at length in his "Touch and Glow" piece. The glowing logo is a fun throwback, but the display is the real story of this generation.

Sources
